exampleAnswers.title: Determining the Existence of a Multiplicative Inverse

question.text: Select the correct options in the reasoning below.
question.explanation:
An integer $a$ has the multiplicative inverse modulo $n$ if and only if $a$ and $n$ are coprime, i.e., $\textrm{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

In our case, $a=15$ and $n=17.$ So, we have

\[ \textrm{gcd}(15,17)=1. \]

Therefore, we conclude the following:

The integer $15$ $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{has}}$ the multiplicative inverse modulo $17$ since $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{gcd}(15,17)}$ $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}= 1}.$

example.title: Determining the Existence of a Multiplicative Inverse

question.text:
Which of the following integers has a multiplicative inverse modulo $50?$

  1. $10$
  2. $33$
  3. $45$
question.explanation:
An integer $a$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $n$ if and only if $a$ and $n$ are coprime, i.e., $\textrm{gcd}(a,n)=1.$

With this in mind, let's examine the given options.

  • $10$ does not have a multiplicative inverse modulo $50$ since $\textrm{gcd}(10,50)=10\neq1. \:\:{\color{red}\times}$

  • $33$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $50$ since $\textrm{gcd}(33,50)=1. \:\:{\color{darkgreen}\checkmark}$

  • $45$ does not have a multiplicative inverse modulo $50$ since $\textrm{gcd}(45,50)=5\neq1. \:\:{\color{red}\times}$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

question.text: Use trial and error to compute the following residue.
question.explanation:
The multiplicative inverse of $4$ modulo $9,$ denoted $4^{-1},$ is the number $x$ such that

\[ 4 \cdot x \equiv 1 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:9). \]

Note that since $\text{gcd}(4,9) = 1,$ an inverse element exists and is unique up to congruence modulo $9.$

Since the modulus $n=9$ is small, we can find the inverse $x$ by computing exponents of $4$ (modulo $9$) until we get a result of $1\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 4^2 &\equiv 4\cdot 4 \equiv 16 \equiv 9 + 7 \equiv 7 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \\[5pt] 4^3 &\equiv 4\cdot 7 \equiv 28 \equiv 3\cdot 9 + 1\equiv 1 && (\textrm{mod}\:9) \end{align*}

So, $4 \cdot 7 \equiv 1 \, (\textrm{mod} \:9).$ Therefore, the multiplicative inverse of $4$ modulo $9$ is $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{7}.$

exampleAnswers.title: Computing Inverses Using the Extended Euclidean Algorithm

question.text: Fill in the blanks to make the following reasoning true.
question.explanation:
First of all, notice that $\textrm{gcd}(62,77)=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1}.$ So, the multiplicative inverse of $62$ modulo $77$ exists.

The multiplicative inverse of $62$ modulo $77$ is the number $x$ such that

\[ 62\cdot x \equiv 1 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:77). \]

To find the value of $x,$ we will use the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

\begin{align*} \begin{matrix} \color{red}77 & = & \color{red}62\cdot 1 & + & \color{red}15 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{blue}62 & = & \color{blue}15 \cdot 4 & + & \color{blue}2 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{black}15 & = & \color{black}2 \cdot 7 & + & \color{black}1 \\ \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

\begin{align*} \color{red}15 &= \color{red} 77 - 62 \\[5pt] \color{blue}2 &= \color{blue} 62 - 15\cdot 4 \\[5pt] 1 &= 15 - 2\cdot 7. \end{align*}

Then, we back-substitute:

\begin{align*} 1 &= 15-{\color{blue}2}\cdot 7 \\[5pt] &= 15-{\color{blue}(62-15\cdot 4)}\cdot 7 \\[5pt] &= 15 - 62\cdot 7 + 15\cdot 28 \\[5pt] &= {\color{red}15} \cdot 29 - 62\cdot 7 \\[5pt] &= {\color{red}(77-62)} \cdot 29 - 62\cdot 7 \\[5pt] &= 77\cdot 29 - 62 \cdot 29 - 62\cdot 7 \\[5pt] &= 62 \cdot (\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-36}) + 77\cdot \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{29} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

We can write this result modulo $77,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 62 \cdot (-36) + 77 \cdot 29& \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:77) \\[5pt] 62 \cdot (-36) & \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:77) \\[5pt] 62 \cdot (77-36) & \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:77) \\[5pt] 62 \cdot 41 & \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:77) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, we have $62\cdot 41\equiv 1 \: (\textrm{mod}\:77),$ which means that $62^{-1} \: \textrm{mod} \: 77=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{41}.$

question.text: Fill in the blanks to make the following reasoning true.
question.explanation:
First of all, notice that $\textrm{gcd}(50,97)=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1}.$ So, the multiplicative inverse of $50$ modulo $97$ exists.

The multiplicative inverse of $50$ modulo $97$ is the number $x$ such that

\[ 50\cdot x \equiv 1 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:97). \]

To find the value of $x,$ we will use the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

\begin{align*} \begin{matrix} \color{red}97& = & \color{red}50\cdot 1 & + & \color{red}47 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{blue}50& = & \color{blue}47\cdot 1 & + & \color{blue}3 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{magenta}47 & = & \color{magenta}3 \cdot 15& + & \color{black}2 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{black}3 & = & \color{black}2 \cdot 1& + & \color{black}1 \\ \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

\begin{align*} \color{red}47 &= \color{red} 97 - 50 \\[5pt] \color{blue}3 &= \color{blue} 50-47 \\[5pt] \color{magenta}2 &= \color{magenta} 47- 3\cdot 15\\[5pt] 1 &= 3-2. \end{align*}

Then, we back-substitute:

\begin{align*} 1 &= 3-{\color{magenta}2} \\[5pt] &= 3-{\color{magenta}(47-3\cdot 15)} \\[5pt] &= {\color{blue}3}\cdot 16 - 47\\[5pt] &= {\color{blue}(50-47)}\cdot 16 - 47 \\[5pt] &= 50\cdot 16 - {\color{red}47}\cdot 17\\[5pt] &= 50\cdot 16 - {\color{red}(97-50)} \cdot 17 \\[5pt] &= 50\cdot 33- 97\cdot 17 \\[5pt] &= 50\cdot \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{33} + 97\cdot (\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-17}) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

We can write this result modulo $97,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 50\cdot 33 + 97\cdot (-17)& \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:97) \\[5pt] 50\cdot 33& \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:97) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, we have $50\cdot 33\equiv 1 \: (\textrm{mod}\:97),$ which means that $50^{-1} \: \textrm{mod} \: 97=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{33}.$

question.text: Fill in the blanks to make the following reasoning true.
question.explanation:
First of all, notice that $\textrm{gcd}(189,281)=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1}.$ So, the multiplicative inverse of $189$ modulo $281$ exists.

The multiplicative inverse of $189$ modulo $281$ is the number $x$ such that

\[ 189\cdot x \equiv 1 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:281). \]

To find the value of $x,$ we will use the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

\begin{align*} \begin{matrix} \color{red}281 & = & \color{red}189\cdot 1 & + & \color{red}92 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{blue}189& = & \color{blue}92 \cdot 2 & + & \color{blue}5 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{magenta}92 & = & \color{magenta}5 \cdot 18 & + & \color{black}2 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{black}5 & = & \color{black}2 \cdot 2& + & \color{black}1 \\ \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

\begin{align*} \color{red}92 &= \color{red} 281 - 189 \\[5pt] \color{blue}5 &= \color{blue} 189 - 92\cdot 2 \\[5pt] \color{magenta}2 &= \color{magenta} 92- 5\cdot 18\\[5pt] 1 &= 5-2\cdot 2. \end{align*}

Then, we back-substitute:

\begin{align*} 1 &= 5-{\color{magenta}2}\cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= 5-{\color{magenta}(92- 5\cdot 18)}\cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= {\color{blue}5}\cdot 37 - 92\cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= {\color{blue}(189 - 92\cdot 2)}\cdot 37 - 92\cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= 189\cdot 37 -{\color{red}92} \cdot 76 \\[5pt] &= 189\cdot 37 - {\color{red}( 281 - 189)} \cdot 76\\[5pt] &= 189 \cdot 113 - 281\cdot 76\\[5pt] &= 189\cdot \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{113} + 281\cdot (\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-76}) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

We can write this result modulo $281,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 189\cdot 113+ 281\cdot (-76)& \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:281) \\[5pt] 189\cdot 113 & \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:281) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, we have $189\cdot 113\equiv 1 \: (\textrm{mod}\:281),$ which means that $189^{-1} \: \textrm{mod} \: 281=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{113}.$

question.text: Fill in the blanks to make the following reasoning true.
question.explanation:
First of all, notice that $\textrm{gcd}(75, 22)=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1}.$ So, the multiplicative inverse of $22$ modulo $75$ exists.

The multiplicative inverse of $22$ modulo $75$ is the number $x$ such that \[ 22 \cdot x \equiv 1 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:75). \]

To find the value of $x,$ we will use the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction: \begin{align*} \begin{matrix} \color{red}75 & = & \color{red}22 \cdot 3 & + & \color{red}9 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{blue}22 & = & \color{blue}9 \cdot 2 & + & \color{blue}4 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{black}9 & = & \color{black}4 \cdot 2 & + & \color{black}1 \\ \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

\begin{align*} \color{red}9 &= \color{red} 75 - 22\cdot 3 \\[5pt] \color{blue}4 &= \color{blue} 22 - 9\cdot 2 \\[5pt] 1 &= 9 - 4\cdot 2. \end{align*}

Then, we back-substitute:

\begin{align*} 1 &= 9-{\color{blue}4}\cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= 9-{\color{blue}(22-9\cdot 2)}\cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= 9 - 22\cdot 2 + 9\cdot 4 \\[5pt] &= {\color{red}9}\cdot 5 - 22\cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= {\color{red}(75 - 22\cdot 3)}\cdot 5 - 22\cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= 75 \cdot 5 - 22\cdot 15 - 22\cdot 2 \\[5pt] &= 75 \cdot 5 - 22\cdot 17 \\[5pt] &= 22\cdot (\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-17}) + 75 \cdot (\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{5}) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

We can write this result modulo $75,$ as follows: \begin{align*} 22 \cdot (-17) + 75 \cdot 5& \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:75) \\[5pt] 22\cdot (-17) & \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:75) \\[5pt] 22\cdot (75-17) & \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:75) \\[5pt] 22\cdot 58& \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:75) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, we have $22\cdot 58\equiv 1 \: (\textrm{mod}\:75),$ which means that $22^{-1} \: \textrm{mod} \: 75=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{58}.$

The multiplicative inverse of $55$ modulo $258$ is the number $x$ such that

\[ 55 \cdot x \equiv 1 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:258). \]

To find the value of $x,$ we will use the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

\begin{align*} \begin{matrix} \color{red}258& = & \color{red}55\cdot 4 & + & \color{red}38 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{blue}55& = & \color{blue}38\cdot 1 & + & \color{blue}17 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{magenta}38& = & \color{magenta}17 \cdot 2 & + & \color{black}4 \\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & \\ \color{black}17 & = & \color{black}4 \cdot 4& + & \color{black}1 \\ \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

\begin{align*} \color{red}38 &= \color{red} 258 - 55\cdot 4 \\[5pt] \color{blue}17 &= \color{blue} 55 - 38 \\[5pt] \color{magenta}4 &= \color{magenta} 38-17\cdot 2\\[5pt] 1 &= 17-4\cdot 4. \end{align*}

Then, we back-substitute:

\begin{align*} 1 &= 17-{\color{magenta}4}\cdot 4 \\[5pt] &= 17-{\color{magenta}(38-17\cdot 2)}\cdot 4 \\[5pt] &= {\color{blue}17}\cdot 9 - 38 \cdot 4 \\[5pt] &= {\color{blue}(55-38)}\cdot 9 - 38 \cdot 4 \\[5pt] &= 55\cdot 9 - {\color{red}38} \cdot 13 \\[5pt] &= 55\cdot 9 - {\color{red}(258 - 55\cdot 4)} \cdot 13 \\[5pt] &= 55\cdot \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{61} + 258\cdot (\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-13}) \end{align*}

We can write this result modulo $258,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 55 \cdot 61 + 258\cdot (-13)& \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:258) \\[5pt] 55\cdot 61& \equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:258) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

So, we have $55\cdot 61\equiv 1 \: (\textrm{mod}\:258),$ which means that $55^{-1} \: \textrm{mod} \: 258 =\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{61}.$
